Finland Reviews Response After 2021 Cyber Attack Disrupted National Power Grid

Finnish authorities and industry leaders are reviewing lessons learned from the major cyber attack that struck Finland’s national power grid in 2021, temporarily disrupting electricity supplies, telecommunications, and payments across the country. While no critical infrastructure has been disrupted since, the incident continues to shape security policy and investment across multiple sectors.

The coordinated attack, which took place in late March 2021, targeted the control systems of Fingrid’s high-voltage transmission network, causing cascading outages that affected businesses and households from Helsinki to Oulu. Telecom networks and digital payments infrastructure, heavily reliant on stable electricity supplies, were also impacted during several hours of rolling blackouts that day.

Metso Oyj, a leading industrial equipment supplier, was among the companies forced to halt production at several facilities as a result of the power cuts. “We lost about eight hours of manufacturing time at our Tampere and Jyväskylä sites,” said Antti Räsänen, Metso’s Chief Security Officer. “Our staff responded quickly, and we avoided long-term damage, but the event highlighted how interdependent our operations are with the national grid.”

The Confederation of Finnish Industries estimated that the event cost the national economy over €120 million in lost output and emergency response expenses. “We saw impacts across manufacturing, logistics, retail, and even healthcare, as backup systems were tested beyond expected durations,” said Mari Koskinen, a spokesperson for the group.

An investigation by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-FI) later revealed that the attack likely originated from outside Finland and exploited outdated software in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems. The government moved quickly to mandate software updates and require multi-factor authentication for remote access to critical infrastructure.

Since the 2021 attack, utilities and industrial firms have stepped up cyber resilience measures. “We’ve accelerated our investments in network segmentation and incident response,” said Räsänen. “We now run quarterly exercises simulating grid failures.”

Regulators also introduced new reporting requirements and increased funding for sector-wide cyber training. The Finnish Energy Authority said in a statement that the crisis “underscored the importance of public-private cooperation in preparing for, detecting, and responding to cyber threats.”

Labour unions applauded the reforms but called for more support for frontline technical staff. “It’s vital that workers responsible for keeping our infrastructure secure have the training and resources they need,” said Jari Mäkelä of the Industrial Workers’ Union.

As Finland continues to digitise its economy, the 2021 cyber attack remains a stark reminder of the vulnerabilities facing modern infrastructure—and the need for ongoing vigilance.
